column2: At a round table on the meaning and titling of works, de Kooning maintains that if an artist can always title his paintings, it is because he is not always very clear.

Two thousand people attend the events celebrating the 200th anniversary of Goethe, a pantheist admired at the Bauhaus and a longtime resident of Weimar; four years after the war, the celebrants affirm that nationality matters less than the contribution to human progress 2000 participants Consequences: the birth of the Aspen Institute's annual summer conference

After her solo retrospective at MoMA (the first of its kind for a textile artist), Anni hopes the museum will buy the wall hanging at a low price; the museum declines. The Busch-Reisinger acquires it soon afterward thanks to a bold curator. the wall hanging had survived the war only because Anni had given it to her parents, who had laid it on their grand piano as a piano cover, with a vase of flowers on top; the ring left by the water is still visible and passes for a calculated compositional element Consequences: a work become a classic, perpetually in demand, but which Harvard rarely lets travel (fragility, institutional whim)

During her exhibition at MoMA in 1949, Anni teaches the principles of weaving; she asks the students to imagine themselves on the coast of Peru centuries ago, without any machine, and to think about how to weave. a primitive loom: parallel twigs evenly spaced, linked by perpendicular strips of leaf; possible materials: animal skins, bird feathers, shredded tree bark, wildflower petals, seaweed Consequences: The student who impressed her most built a miniature loom with the matches from an ordinary matchbook.

At his exhibition in Paris the year before the article (1950), Hofmann buys recent Dubuffets there, hung at his home among French primitives and his own canvases. Paintings hung in his Provincetown house and his New York studio.

Kline visits a friend who enlarges his own sketches with a Bell-Opticon; the friend asks whether he has any small drawings in his pocket — Franz always does. They see the sketches magnified “bodilessly” against the wall: a 4-by-5-inch drawing of a rocking chair becomes gigantic black brushstrokes in which the image is erased by the strokes themselves. sketches of 4×5 inches (about 10×13 cm); he feeds drawing after drawing into the projector Consequences: a total, instant conversion of his style: large canvases, house painters' brushes, hardware-store enamels

On the day Dreier returns to the campus, Nell Rice, spokeswoman for the group (a narrow majority of the faculty), asks him to cut all ties with the college: it must live, but not with him in an administrative or policy role. Dreier, stunned, asks that the request be put in writing. Consequences: The start of the final crisis.

A majority of students sign a petition asking Dreier to bow to the majority of the faculty — among them students of Albers himself. Against all expectations, Dreier proposes to hand over his responsibilities to N. O. Pittenger, who has just arrived to discuss the post of administrator. Consequences: Dreier agrees to leave.

Pittenger, unhappy with the earlier management of the annuities, refuses to commit himself until the question is cleared up; accusations of misappropriation arise because Dreier had put the bonds in Albers's name alone and Albers had just asked that Dreier be included in the fund. Professor Cole, the longtime auditor, comes to the college and reassures everyone about the legality of the arrangement; for lack of immediate money, Dreier secures only 80% of the funds, the college promising the remaining 20% later. $300 a year in government bonds since 1944 for Albers, Jalowetz, and Straus (fifty years old and five years of teaching); 80/20%. Consequences: Pittenger accepts an advisory role; the resignations become final.

On behalf of a group of colleagues, the secretary Mangold writes a long typed letter: Dreier has spoken of taking back the rectorship; the objections: confusion about the college's direction, inability to conduct a meeting, autocracy, exclusion of others from his deliberations, a demoralizing economic pessimism. A handwritten note added: “I think he is largely unconscious of these things. That he is psychically unbalanced.” She implores Albers to dissuade Dreier, to avoid an open, explosive, and useless controversy. A typed letter with a handwritten note; “he is psychically unbalanced” Consequences: Albers is not persuaded

Less than a week after Mangold's letter, at a meeting in New York with potential trustees of Black Mountain, Albers announces that Dreier has decided not to leave the college. Consequences: Two weeks of uncertainty

In a handwritten postscript, Albers urgently asks that Dreier be relieved as soon as possible of the burden of treasurer in the present surroundings, where his friends are of little help; he proposes that Pittenger suggest someone else if he cannot come himself, while assuring him of their confidence. A handwritten note, “a PS.... close to my heart”

Pittenger calls his four days a most interesting experience: Albers, an exceptionally good art teacher, is as impossible as an executive as he is great as an artist; Dreier has done good work with the students and the buildings but does not remember his promises from one day to the next and has lost everyone's confidence — largely, according to Pittenger, because of his relationship with a woman who is a “teacher in the Art School”: the students reproach him not so much for the mistress as for the fact that she is on the payroll. “teacher in the Art School”; a salaried mistress; a judgment on Albers Consequences: Reveals the college's tolerance of open relationships

Tolk-Watkins sends Asawa an advertising brochure for buying a house in Sausalito, marked to show the location of the Tin Angel and their cottage, with a sarcastic “ha !” next to the word “homes”. Letter dated January 28, 1949; Sausalito's billing: “city of homes [and] gateway to the redwood empire” Consequences: Confronts Asawa with the expectations of postwar domesticity
In a letter to Peggy Tolk-Watkins, Asawa says she understands Trude Guermonprez and her multiple desires better and better.

After the lecture and its fiery denunciations, beautiful women pass baskets around to collect dollar bills; the money buys liquor in paper cups, then dancing to polkas for hours Words: Elaine: half an inch in a paper cup … very, very festive Atmosphere: smoke, coffee, voices, polkas Stakes: the artists' community finances itself

Bill and an unknown artist, drunk on sherry, go down to the beach despite hurricane warnings; the man passes out; Sanders and Bill carry him toward the water and strip, having no bathing suits; a state policeman arrests them; a cell until they sober up, a five-dollar fine. Atmosphere: hurricane wind, burlesque drama Stakes: Elaine's worry about Bill; the grotesque as a way of life.

At the end of the summer, a general hangover and gossip; her housemate finally asks Elaine how she keeps her calm; a curt answer. Words: Never. She would not allow it. Stakes: Elaine's vital wager against melancholy.

A dinner among artists; Grillo serves a meat-flavored dish that he will later admit was local whiting; Freilicher brings Basie records and tomatoes from the garden; Elaine monopolizes the conversation with verve. Words: Elaine talks about everything, from drawing to the death penalty (Rivers). Atmosphere: a happily besieged community

Gropius proposes a mural; Albers, at first not much interested, decides to make a mural of truth: choosing Flemish bond, refusing colors and reliefs, keeping the gray, recessing calibrated voids (brick lengths, halves, quarters) to compose with shadows, aiming at lightness and an effect of growth; he names the wall América. Words: “un mural de verdad, en el que se respetara y preservara el murus” Atmosphere: Diffuse light from distant windows on the gray brick Stakes: Asserting a North American conception of the mural against the Mexican school

Schauffler bets Rondthaler two quarts of beer that he will not move to Oregon; Rondthaler takes up the challenge, goes, finds a job with the Forest Service, enters Reed College, and spends a lifetime there. Words: “In 1949 Manvel Schauffler bet me two quarts of beer I would not move to Oregon” Atmosphere: the complicity of former students, postwar insouciance Stakes: a friend's bet decides a whole life

Fuller co-opts a student whose voice impresses him to read one of his 200-page poems; the guests doze off after the first hours; Fuller, cheerful, insists that the reading go on to the end Atmosphere: An interminable evening, a vaguely comic solemnity, Fuller's radiant obstinacy Stakes: Egocentric genius facing an exhausted community

Believing he had a firm offer, Wolpert has resigned his post; Natasha's letter cancels everything; he replies with a diatribe (a fraudulent college, a disgusting double-cross); Natasha speaks of a misunderstanding; a few days later, he dies of polio Words: “I want to hear nothing further from your fraudulent college… you have sunk to your true level” Atmosphere: Rage, betrayal, the tragic irony of death Stakes: The power struggles of a college on the brink crush even its own children

Two weeks after the launch, the first critique session; the critics move from team to team; Albers talks with the students from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m. with Switzer; almost all propose a monumental setting without having thought about the plastic; in the evening, Albers writes of his exasperation to Anni, noting Kahn's absence. Words: Albers to Anni: “Quite soon struggle as almost all propose a tremendous 'setting' for plastics. But without thinking of plastics. And Kahn the coordinator, though here, did not show up. We are wondering.” Atmosphere: A long afternoon, the students' confusion, Albers's restrained disappointment. Stakes: A silent confrontation of two pedagogies: the hand against the concept; the absent man who was supposed to lead.

At the end of September or early October, before leaving for Cincinnati, Kahn visits Albers to discuss the plastics problem; Albers shows him for the first time his geometric line drawings — the future Structural Constellations; the conversation is undocumented. Atmosphere: Two men discovering each other; the authors invite us to imagine the exchange. Stakes: The crossing of two major trajectories of modernism around impossible spatial structures.

After their summer in Asheville, the Woelffers pass through New York; Pollock, sharing their passions, urges them to stay and look for a permanent gallery. Words: Pollock begs them to stay (paraphrased). Stakes: A choice between a New York career and an itinerant life.

The architect Williams designs the building in consultation with Turner, who finances it in part through a loan to the college and has the workshop and kiln built, without getting involved in the internal struggles of a college in full transition after Albers's resignation. Words: Turner: it was not a time of discovery but of consolidating what he had learned at Alfred Atmosphere: hardworking solitude, outdoors in a field Stakes: A traditional craftsman let loose in the most experimental college in America

Eleanor poses with her back turned in the ballroom with walls painted by Weber; open flash of the 8x10 camera; four variations kept in the printing: the chignon comes undone, the arms bend out of the frame, drop, spread over the radiator. Words: Callahan: Eleanor did not know what Weber was talking about with his painting, or she would not have let him do it. Atmosphere: Relaxed, spontaneous, by day as by night. Stakes: The couple's intimacy as an artistic laboratory.

Asawa in a black dress sewn by Johanna Jalowetz from a fabric of Anni Albers's; Schlesinger at the piano; Asawa stumbles over her vows, everyone laughs, the baby Ragland crawls on the floor; then a sober reception of cold cuts and champagne facing the double view of ocean and bay Words: Lanier later: they were all laughing, and they were crying and laughing, and they got through it Atmosphere: Warm, disorderly, burlesque and moved Stakes: The union of two Black Mountain alumni among friends from the college, Fuller's Dymaxion ring as a symbol

The faculty, by a narrow majority of one vote, forces the departure of the acting treasurer Theodore Dreier, a cofounder, with the assent of a large share of the students; Josef and Anni Albers and several other teachers resign in solidarity. Atmosphere: A governance crisis within a community supposed to live by consensus Stakes: The break after sixteen years of life at the college; the end of the Albers era

In the outbuilding built in memory of Mark Dreier, Rauschenberg photographs a chair under a diagonal light grazing a white plaster wall — a purity and precision that Albers could not wring out of him elsewhere. Atmosphere: Silence, stillness, dust, the aural superimposed on the visual Stakes: Photography as a premonition of the White Paintings and of 4'33"

At the 1949 Mardi Gras, Ingeborg Lauterstein wears a unicorn costume designed by Rauschenberg; Trude Guermonprez photographs her. The photo is preserved in the Black Mountain College Papers of the North Carolina State Archives. Atmosphere: Celebration, extravagant costume Stakes: The college's festive and creative spirit, collaboration among artists

Weil and Rauschenberg deliver a group of Albers's paintings; Egan turns on the gallery lights and reveals an exhibition of Franz Kline Words: Weil: “I felt like I had been socked in the stomach”; what they had learned at art school suddenly seemed invalid Atmosphere: Shock and exhilaration Stakes: Swinging from Albers's teaching to the freedom of Abstract Expressionism

The quivering student holds out his long, very bad poem about an existential lawnmower; Olson, visibly at a loss, hands it back to him; M.C., her voice hardened, insists that he keep it and read it; Olson whispers his agreement Words: M.C.: “It's a poem… Fielding wrote it for you… Don't you think you might keep it, and read it?”; Olson: “Yes, of course” Atmosphere: The anxious misery of the nineteen-year-old, the master's embarrassment Stakes: A humiliated young poet rescued by an ally

Dawson sits down near Olson after the others have left; Olson is talking to a woman student, his face six inches from hers; he breaks a hot dog in two, dips one half in the mustard, tears a roll into quarters and then into crumbs, grabs a tomato across the table and bites into it, scoops up potato chips by the fistful, all the while talking about Howard Fast, Saroyan, Pound, Eliot, Wolfe, a cigarette in his mouth and a glass of milk in hand; at the end, only a few lettuce leaves remain. Words: He talks about Howard Fast, Saroyan, Ezra Pound, T.S. Eliot, Thomas Wolfe Atmosphere: young Dawson's fascination before this titanic giant Stakes: the narrator's initiation into the Olson character

A full-dress questionnaire: Wolfe? “No good, bad on public morals.” Saroyan? “No good.” Scholem Asch? “No good.” Seeing Dawson's crestfallen face, Olson rests his elbow on his shoulder, takes an enormous drag, winks, and delivers his verdict, then walks off with an enormous laugh. Words: “Every dog has his own fleas” Atmosphere: comic, affectionate, overwhelming Stakes: literary taste as a lesson in authority

After the prototype test of the summer of 1948, Fuller returns in 1949 and succeeds in raising a self-supporting geodesic structure; Nakagawa photographs Fuller with the model Atmosphere: The convinced euphoria of the geodesic proselyte Stakes: The redemption of the inventor of the Dymaxion failures through a tangible success

The student presents a column about a foot high: two perpendicular wooden crosses, the upper one suspended in the air by taut nylon threads, a rigid balance maintained by outer threads; Fuller at once reads in it a new principle of engineering and asks for a modified version. Atmosphere: A decisive click — a student inspires the master. Stakes: The authorship of a discovery (tensegrity) that will also be fought out before the patent offices.

With ID students who have come from Chicago with Fuller, the aluminum-tube dome prepared for the Pentagon is raised; as it rises, the lattice becomes stronger than its parts; the transparent heat-welded plastic skin is then tested. Atmosphere: The triumph of a “synergetic” process after the previous year's failure. Stakes: The validation of tensegrity and of all of Fuller's total thinking.

Fuller hands his students an apocalypse problem: the city is evacuated, all concentrations of 50,000 people or more are in immediate danger of annihilation, consumer goods are diverted to decentralized communities, everything not decentralized will be destroyed. Words: “The city is to be evacuated… Everything not decentralized will be destroyed.” Atmosphere: Eschatological urgency; nuclear fear turned into a design exercise. Stakes: The transformation of nuclear terror into technocratic planning.

After the request for Dreier's resignation and Albers's protest resignation, Trayer and Goldowski, acting officers, propose bringing back Rice — the man who held the community together longer than anyone; Aydelotte opposes it; Rice does not pursue it. Words: Aydelotte: “Nothing would be more disastrous for the college.”; Rice: “For a moment the clouds seemed to open.” Atmosphere: A cracked community, a fleeting hope. Stakes: The founder's missed return.

Tired of cafeterias, a group of painters decides one evening to rent a loft; twenty founding members each pay ten dollars; unable to find a name, they simply call it “the Club”; there they drink coffee and a few drinks and talk into the night. Words: De Kooning: the Greeks and Italians have their social clubs along Eighth Avenue; they wanted nothing to do with art. Atmosphere: Immigrant conviviality, a refusal of institutional seriousness. Stakes: The underground institutionalization of the New York avant-garde.

Kline drops in on a friend who enlarges his own sketches in a Bell-Opticon; the friend asks whether he has any small drawings on him — Franz pulls out a handful; projection on the wall; the 4×5-inch rocking chair becomes gigantic black strokes that erase the image; he goes from drawing to drawing, the image always swallowed by the strokes that delimit it. Words: The friend asks whether he has some of those little drawings in his pocket Atmosphere: the two men's shared astonishment at the change of scale Stakes: an instant conversion that grounds all of Kline's later art

On the very day of Dreier's return, Nell Rice, spokeswoman for the five dissidents (a narrow majority), explains to him that the college must go on, but not with him in any administrative or decision-making role; Dreier, stunned, asks that it be put in writing. Words: Rice: the college cannot succeed as long as Dreier serves in an administrative capacity; Dreier: let the request be put to him in writing. Atmosphere: Shock, head-on, tense Stakes: The cofounder dismissed by his own faculty

After Pittenger agrees to handle the transition, the Alberses, Schlesinger, and Guermonprez make their resignations public, joined by Dreier; Albers tells his colleagues that he will continue his classes until the end of the semester but has ceased to belong to the college. Words: “I will continue my classes, but do not consider me tomorrow a member of this place.” Atmosphere: A bitter but dignified break, after crisis upon crisis. Stakes: The end of sixteen years of Albers's total involvement in the community.

Intimidated at the idea of writing about the man who had been her teacher months earlier, she fills a third of the article with quotations from Albers, then elegantly refutes his formula “My work is study, not revelation,” declaring that revelation dwells in “the austere expressions of his spaces and colors”; the same issue contains nineteen of her reviews 19 reviews in one issue; she will claim a record of 38 reviews a month Consequences: Elaine's first text on Albers

Elaine publishes in ARTnews reviews of Albers's exhibition shown in two galleries, then the article “Albers Paints a Picture”. Consequences: Turns the admiration born at Black Mountain into critical writing.

Williams discovers Lou Harrison at the premiere of Ives's First Sonata, played by William Masselos from a score edited and reconstructed by Harrison from an old manuscript and sketches. Riegger and Varèse deeply moved in the audience; Williams imagines Thomson, Copland, Cowell, and Bernstein there without having seen them. Consequences: One of the greatest piano moments Williams ever heard, still felt 53 years later.

Resignation in February. A summer trip to forget teaching, administration, and community life for a while (letter to Grote, March 31, 1949). Josef gives four design seminars at the university in Mexico City (June 10-August 15); lodging at Avenida Veracruz 102 C, Colonia Roma. The Moellenhoffs visit them and they travel together for three weeks; a visit to Diego Rivera's Anahuacalli museum with Rivera and Clara Porset. Consequences: The final departure from BMC

Students in the fall of 1948 find a decimated faculty; Frank, exhausted by the acrimonious meetings, finds a better post in Quogue; Ann follows him shortly afterward. Frank and Nell come home late and exhausted from endless faculty meetings. Consequences: The mountains exchanged for the ocean.

In February 1949, she joins the small chorus led by Bimbus, who draws more musicality out of them than they thought they had. Invited to sing one Sunday at the Black YMCA in Asheville: they give fragments of a Bach cantata; the local choir answers with spirituals of a rich, deep Black sound, including “I Been 'Buked and I Been Scorned,” which touches them to the bone; then shared refreshments. a Sunday; a Bach cantata (which one forgotten); the spiritual “I Been 'Buked and I Been Scorned” Consequences: A memorable experience of encounter and of Black music

A teachers' petition asks Albers for a faculty meeting with a view to requesting T. Dreier's resignation; Dreier forestalls it by resigning; the resignations of the Alberses and others, dated February 18, 1949, are in the archives, but the student petition described by several witnesses cannot be found. Consequences: The leadership overturned
Mel Mitchell Kelly asserts that the Rondthalers and the Levis, still officially members of the faculty, cabled their proxies against Dreier; Mary Caroline Richards has absolutely no memory of it.

The Alberses resign in early February 1949; the break, in the making since at least 1947, perhaps 1945, is attributed to their solidarity with Ted Dreier, around whom all of the college's pathologies had crystallized. Consequences: The end of the Alberses' presence after almost 16 years

Dissident teachers petition for a meeting aimed at requesting Dreier's resignation; he forestalls it by resigning; the Alberses and others also submit their resignations on February 18, 1949. Atmosphere: a tense show of force, later remembered in contradictory ways Stakes: the seizure of power and the selective blindness of memory

For days, Bill talks, Elaine notes down his ideas, they go over the text again and again, she makes suggestions; in the end, Bill states something totally right, leaving no room for argument. Words: Elaine: “Bill never liked to write. He talked and I took down his ideas for him.” Atmosphere: A literary workshop for two, the couple's creative complicity. Stakes: Bill's fame is built in Elaine's shadow, she not recognized as his equal.

She informs Albers that she is leaving ARTnews to travel to Tangier with her sister Marjorie: the idea of doing nothing but paint by the Mediterranean appeals to her; the plan remains a passing fantasy, but she stops writing short reviews, fearing she will lose the “rough edges” an artist needs, since a critic must look at everything evenhandedly letter to Albers, March 1949 Consequences: she moves on to feature articles paid up to 75 dollars apiece

The Pittenger-Trayer correspondence (March 25 and 30, 1949) documents the sale of gravel and the Forbes affair; Fuller left a remark about the plumbing in a three-page note dated June 1, 1949; Dreier-Pittenger letters of September 1949. Fuller's 3-page note; gravel from the site Consequences: The financial fragility of 1949

After her noticed photographic work in the summer of 1948, the Board of Fellows invites her to become lecturer in photography for the coming year. Consequences: The first official teaching post in photography

Elaine writes to Albers: she mentions his imminent departure from Black Mountain (announced in March 1949) and her reviews of his double exhibition, published in February, and thanks him for a birthday present (March 12). Atmosphere: Affection and gratitude at a distance, torn between the college and New York. Stakes: The Elaine-Albers bond survives the master's departure and the end of the summer of 1948.

Invited on a five-day camping trip along the ridges, cut short by a day because of frozen toes (she wears only sneakers); rain for the first three days, snow on the fourth, fog almost continuously, no view; a sixty-five-pound pack, sore muscles but a mind dazzled by the virgin trees, the spongy moss, the streams; the last night under an overhanging rock, waking under snow, violets frozen like perfect glass; one night the moon breaks through the clouds and they sing as they walk “Sleepers Awake” and other Bach chorales. a 65-pound (~29 kg) pack; sneakers; rain for 3 days, snow on the 4th; violets frozen into glass; back at the college in the sun with snow still on the packs Consequences: She learns survival, and that physical pain can be dissociated from joy, wonder, and friendship

The four who resigned stay until June to honor their teaching commitments; Dreier, with no classes, leaves Black Mountain for good in mid-April, going to Florida with his wife and then camping out west. Consequences: The end of the Albers-Dreier era.

Having accepted an advisory role with Pittenger, Dreier, with no classes under way, leaves the college for good in mid-April; the Alberses, Trude Guermonprez, and Charlotte Schlesinger stay until June to finish their teaching A trip to Florida, then camping in the West — his first real rest in twenty-five years Consequences: The end of the presence of the founding group of 1933 (except Nell Rice)

An unsigned article (in fact written by Lanier) on Black Mountain College's student project, the Minimum House, illustrated with Hazel Archer's photographs; John Entenza had contacted Lanier and Asawa about this publication on the recommendation of Anni and Josef Albers. Arts and Architecture, April 1949, pp. 30-31 Consequences: The college's work in architecture made known nationally

Lanier gives a vase to his cousin Laurie Pearson, who replies at the end of April that she will never dare put flowers in it. Laurie Pearson's letter of April 30, 1949: “my pond-farm-piece is wonderful. I fear I'll never put flowers in it—it is too beautiful without them”

Breton delivers an anti-American diatribe (racism toward Black people and Indians, sexual hypocrisy, Coca-Cola, the grip on Latin America) at a meeting against dictatorship and war held by the Rassemblement démocratique révolutionnaire. The RDR, an anticapitalist and anti-Stalinist movement. Consequences: An index of French anxiety in the face of postwar American power.
One night of the camping trip, the moon breaks through the clouds; walking along the forest road, they sing “Sleepers Awake” and other Bach chorales Atmosphere: magical, detached from physical pain

Dissatisfied with her review after a whole day in Nakian's studio, she stays to work at the office after everyone has left, toward the 5 p.m. deadline; Hess arrives at nine in the morning just as she is leaving and asks suspiciously: “You haven't been here all night, have you?”; she laughs weakly and flees without answering a 5 p.m. deadline; a whole night at the office Consequences: an illustration of her relentless demands on herself

After Subjects of the Artist dissolves in May 1949, Tony Smith and a few artists take over the lease of the loft at 35 East Eighth Street and continue the series of Friday evening lectures, named Studio 35 after the address. (Note the inconsistency in the source: it dates Bill's lecture to February 1949, before this dissolution.) the loft at 35 East Eighth Street; Friday evening lectures Consequences: Continuity of the avant-garde's forum.

With the 5 p.m. deadline approaching, she hands in her other reviews, announces a few touch-ups to the Nakian article, and gets down to it; she suddenly realizes that everyone has left; she works all night; at nine in the morning, she runs into Hess coming in Words: Hess, suspicious: “You haven't been here all night, have you?”; she laughs weakly at so grotesque a suggestion and flees without answering Atmosphere: the office's nighttime solitude, dawn, comedy Stakes: demands on herself to the point of exhaustion
Six months after the brochure, Asawa settles in San Francisco and brushes against bohemian circles. Consequences: The beginning of her Californian life

Having agreed to be general adviser, Pittenger becomes rector in July 1949, the faculty granting him all administrative prerogatives so that he can act without hindrance, while the search for a permanent incumbent continues

His first trip in a sleeping car (a Pullman), an almost empty car, well padded, the air slowed down, lukewarm; in a kind of haze a voice tells him that he is going toward a place and that he will change; he panics but desires it; later, reading that what does not change is the will to change, he knows he has found his man (Olson). An almost empty Pullman car, serene, warm

The first article in the series “X Paints a Picture”: Dickinson, 57, astonishingly little known and underappreciated; she compares in detail three states of The Ruin; a year earlier she had painted The Music Party, showing him at the violin with Daniel Brustlein on the cello a series documented by the photographer Rudy Burckhardt; Dickinson aged 57 Consequences: the launch of the series that will make her reputation

The course in pre-architectural composition takes the name Composición Pura: the intuitive and abstract character of the composition of three-dimensional space based on material, form, and color, as a habit prior to architectural realization. The sequence: plans, model, critique, surveying of the model from the plans, group critique. The difference from Albers's course: exercises in predetermined spaces. Published in Arquitectura y Construcción no. 16, September 1949

Wyeth sees Ben Loper in front of his cabin while driving home, comes back two days later, and discovers the scene: Loper sitting alone in the dark room, a triangle of yellow light around one eye. Five months of work, eleven weeks of them in execution. a month before Loper, a greenhouse worker, agrees to pose on weekends; a gesso panel of about 27 x 17 inches Consequences: the title found during a sitting

Two days after their meeting on the road, Wyeth knocks at the cabin door; invited in, he opens it on Loper sitting alone in the half-dark, leaning forward, a triangle of light around one eye; Loper gets up and the vision vanishes — Wyeth will never see that patch of light again. Atmosphere: the heat of the afternoon, golden dust, a dark room, desolation Stakes: the instant birth of a painting that will require five months of reconstruction from memory

Six former students (including Steinau and Howard), plus Pittenger and Corkran, meet for two days at Forbes's house to propose a reorganization: a Board of Overseers sharing the power to choose a rector (and alone empowered to dismiss him), managing salaries, tenure, budget, and hiring with the rector, and taking an interest in fund-raising; property and educational policy would remain with the faculty. a group of six former students + Pittenger + Corkran, two days of meetings Consequences: The start of a year of community debates

Forbes offers to finance the construction of a new science building up to 6000 dollars and stops at the college during his vacation to help resolve the debates; he says he favors Levi's idea of adding five or six nonresidents to the present Board and would agree to sit on it. 6000 dollars; five to six nonresidents; meetings possibly once or twice a year Consequences: Shows that interest without official power is possible

On a vacation trip, Forbes stops at the college, offers to finance the science building, says he favors Levi's plan, and proposes to look for a rector in parallel with the faculty Words: he says he is inclined to favor Levi's idea Atmosphere: calm, conciliatory Stakes: showing that one can serve without dominating

In Steichen's exhibition, two works by Archer hung close to each other: on the left, Asawa in profile before the doors of the Quiet House; on the right, a smaller close-up of a door handle whose screws form a face Atmosphere: The intimate world of North Carolina carried into the New York galleries Stakes: The “amateur” Hazel-Frieda Larsen exhibited alongside Lange and Levitt

During a sketching session, a simpleminded boy visits Loper; in an hour he goes to open the door and look outside some twenty times; Wyeth finally asks him what he is looking for; his incongruous answer becomes the title of the painting: A Crow Flew By. Words: Wyeth asks the boy what he is looking for; an unrelated answer that becomes the title Atmosphere: absurd, close to unbearable for the concentrating painter Stakes: the chance of a word supplies the title and the meaning of the work

At two in the morning, Wyeth suddenly remembers the beam of light falling on the eye and quickly makes a sketch emphasizing the shadow crossing the face; in it he fixes the final size of the head and decides to reduce the figure in the composition. Atmosphere: the nighttime solitude of a painter who nonetheless works only by day Stakes: the return of the founding vision

A group exhibition organized by Edward Steichen; Archer, presented as a “young amateur” under the name Hazel-Frieda Larsen, contributes seven portrait studies; two photos of the Quiet House hung side by side: Asawa in profile before the doors, and a close-up of a door handle 7 portraits; the right-hand photo slightly smaller; the screws of the handle figure a face with two eyes and a mouth Consequences: New York recognition of Archer's work

A group exhibition of photographs under Steichen's direction: Bourke-White, Levitt, Lange, Hoban, Bubley, and Hazel-Frieda Larsen (Archer). The press release describes her as a “young amateur” presenting “portrait studies”. press release: “She is a polio patient, and during her convalescence has done some of her photography from a wheelchair”; she is then teaching at Black Mountain College and becoming known for her revealing close-ups of faces

Exasperated by the faculty's slowness (a two-thirds vote was needed to change the bylaws), and having run the college during the six months of crisis after the Albers-Dreier resignations, Pittenger resigns, although the Board offers to extend him for a year. a two-thirds majority required to amend the bylaws Consequences: The start of a double search for a rector (Forbes and a faculty committee)

A group exhibition bringing together local artists, sponsoring companies, and institutions to spot talents transferable to industry; the prize included a commission from the sponsoring company. Asawa submits five wallpaper designs; Guermonprez also takes part. Five wallpaper designs.

Among the belongings Albers leaves behind are 2,000 feet of yellow-pine flooring that he wants the college to sell as his agent; the college refuses this responsibility. 2000 (linear) feet of yellow-pine flooring; letters from Warrington to Albers (Dec. 2, 1949) and from Albers to the treasurer (July 3, 1950) Consequences: A lasting dispute over Albers's property

Invited to speak at Studio 35, Bill insists that Motherwell, then in Boston, come down to deliver the lecture, which Elaine cowrote; Bill and Elaine, like other members of the Club, cannot resist coming to hear it Consequences: a symptom of the quarrels between Surrealist and downtown factions

She tells Albers she wants to include his color theories; he replies that he is going to make the series Homage to the Square “based on color”; two weeks later he has finished about a hundred paintings of the same format; she describes the aseptic, almost militant simplicity born of calculations on graph paper and oil sketches, and perceives the unavowed sensitivity of lines that are “peculiarly gentle and tentative” and the translucent atmosphere of the matte colors about 100 paintings in two weeks, all the same size Consequences: she writes about the works for which Albers remains known

Elaine undertakes a long article on Albers and wants to include his color theories in it; Albers replies that he is going to make a series, Homage to the Square, based on color. Two weeks later he has finished some hundred canvases of the same format. about 100 paintings, all the same size, produced in two weeks; calculations on graph paper, oil sketches Consequences: Elaine writes about the works for which Albers remains best known; she describes their aseptic, almost militant simplicity and their unavowed sensitivity

After extending her summer in Provincetown into the fall (working without heat, then a streptococcal infection and a return to New York), Elaine squats in turn in Edwin Denby's apartment on West 21st Street, then in the painter Bill Brown's studio on 100th Street, woken every morning by “dirty ditties” sung by kids on the steps. She claims to have occupied eight studios in 1950. West 21st Street; 100th Street; eight studios in a year; a streptococcal infection

At Pollock's fourth solo show at Betty Parsons's, Elaine disparages all the canvases but one — out of loyalty to Bill or sincere skepticism — within earshot of Greenberg and Krasner, his most fervent defenders.

The previous summer, as Excavation was leaving for Venice, Elaine told Bill that it reminded her of Brueghel's Triumph of Death; he then showed her the magazine whose cover reproduced that painting — she was right, as usual. a magazine cover reproducing Brueghel

Matter, who is renting a room for August, invites Elaine; the invitation charms her because the setting sounds fantastically uncivilized and promises to stir up trouble with certain raving harpies (unidentified women Matter had complained about).

Two years after the Black Mountain summer, having become dean of the design department at Yale, Albers invites Bill to lead twice-weekly crits for the painting students; Bill gives up after two semesters. Elaine, a visiting lecturer at Yale in 1967, will like teaching much more than he did. Crits twice a week; stopped after two semesters; Elaine invited to Yale in 1967 Consequences: A lasting contrast between Elaine's taste for teaching and Bill's rejection of it.

Josef accepts the chairmanship of Yale's design department; the Alberses settle in New Haven. Collaboration on the interiors of the Harvard Graduate Center: Josef designs the brick wall America (Harkness Commons), Anni fabrics for the student residence.

The Homage to the Square series continues; Josef becomes chairman of Yale's design department, a move to New Haven. Work for the Harvard Graduate Center: the brick wall America (Harkness Commons) by Josef, textiles for the dormitories by Anni.

Robert Turner comes with a kiln builder to set up the pottery studio: two or three wheels, an oil kiln and an electric kiln, central tables, shelves, an alcove for materials, a view of the hayfields and the mountains. 2-3 wheels, an oil kiln + an electric kiln, a view of the fields Consequences: Richards becomes a potter there

On his last day, Tommy Jackson takes him to the top of Mount Mitchell in a Model A Ford to see the sunrise; later Wes Huss, Charles Olson, Fee Dawson, and a few others see him off with the Jennerjahns. A Model A Ford; sunrise on Mount Mitchell Consequences: Olson: “Well, there goes the last of the old guard”
